items.followUp: Explain how an enzyme acts on its substrate.

rubric.why: Identifies how a substrate binds to an enzyme.
rubric.description: Substrate binds at the enzyme’s active site, forming an enzyme–substrate complex.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly describing substrate binding at the active site or the enzyme–substrate complex.

rubric.why: Shows the outcome of enzyme action and that the enzyme can act again.
rubric.description: The substrate is converted into product(s), which leave; the enzyme remains unchanged.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the formation/release of product(s) and the enzyme remaining unchanged.

modelAnswer: The substrate binds to the enzyme at its active site, forming an enzyme–substrate complex.
The enzyme converts the substrate into product(s), which are released; the enzyme remains unchanged and can be reused.

items.followUp: What products are formed during alcoholic fermentation?

rubric.why: Identifies the process as the anaerobic breakdown of glucose.
rubric.description: Alcoholic fermentation is the anaerobic breakdown of glucose.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that glucose is broken down without oxygen.

rubric.why: Names the characteristic products of alcoholic fermentation.
rubric.description: It produces ethanol (alcohol) and carbon dioxide.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming both products.

modelAnswer: Alcoholic fermentation is the anaerobic breakdown of glucose, usually by yeast.
It produces ethanol (alcohol) and carbon dioxide, releasing energy.

items.followUp: What are micronutrients? Give two examples.

rubric.why: Distinguishes macronutrients by the relatively large amount required.
rubric.description: Macronutrients are nutrients or mineral elements required in large amounts for plant growth and development.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that they are required in large amounts.

rubric.why: Requires examples of macronutrients.
rubric.description: Examples include nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium and sulfur.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving any two correct examples.

modelAnswer: Macronutrients are nutrients or mineral elements that plants require in large amounts for growth and development.
Examples include nitrogen and phosphorus.

rubric.why: Shows that a source supplies food for transport.
rubric.description: A source is a plant part where sugars are made or released for transport, such as a photosynthesising leaf.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining source as a site that supplies sugars/food.

rubric.why: Shows that a sink receives food from a source.
rubric.description: A sink is a plant part that uses or stores the transported sugars, such as a root, fruit or growing region.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining sink as a site that uses or stores sugars/food.

modelAnswer: A source is a plant part where sugars are made or released for transport, for example, a photosynthesising leaf.
A sink is a plant part that uses or stores transported sugars, for example, a root, fruit or growing region.

items.followUp: Describe four other careers related to biology.

rubric.why: Recognises a biology-based career and its work.
rubric.description: Medicine: applying biological knowledge to diagnose, prevent or treat disease.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid career with a relevant description.

rubric.why: Recognises a career applying biology to crop production.
rubric.description: Agriculture: using biology to improve crops, crop yield or farming practices.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid career with a relevant description.

rubric.why: Recognises a career involving the care or production of fish.
rubric.description: Fisheries: managing or breeding fish and other aquatic resources.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid career with a relevant description.

rubric.why: Allows another correctly described biology-related career.
rubric.description: A further relevant career may include forestry, animal husbandry, veterinary science, biotechnology or pharmacy, with its biological application explained.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for another valid career with a relevant description. The student should name five careers in total; award marks for up to four correctly described careers.

modelAnswer: Medicine: biologists and medical professionals use biological knowledge to diagnose, prevent and treat disease.
Agriculture: biological knowledge is used to improve crops, farming practices and crop yields.
Animal husbandry: biology is applied to the breeding, feeding and care of livestock.
Fisheries: biology is used to manage, breed and raise fish and other aquatic resources.
Forestry: biology helps in the conservation and management of forests and forest resources.

items.followUp: Draw and label a chloroplast, showing its main parts.

rubric.why: Identifies the two membranes surrounding a mitochondrion.
rubric.description: Mitochondrion has an outer membrane and an inner membrane.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for showing or naming both membranes.

rubric.why: Identifies the folds of the inner membrane.
rubric.description: The inner membrane is folded into cristae.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for showing or naming cristae.

rubric.why: Identifies the internal fluid-filled region.
rubric.description: The space enclosed by the inner membrane is the matrix.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for showing or naming the matrix.

rubric.why: States the mitochondrion’s major function.
rubric.description: Mitochondria are the sites of aerobic cellular respiration and energy release, with ATP produced.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking mitochondria with cellular respiration or ATP/energy production.

rubric.why: Checks that the diagram is a recognisable, adequately labelled mitochondrion.
rubric.description: Diagram is recognisable and clearly labels the outer membrane, inner membrane, cristae and matrix.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a clear, correctly labelled diagram; labels may be shown with arrows.

modelAnswer: A mitochondrion is a cell organelle surrounded by two membranes.
The outer membrane is smooth; the inner membrane is folded inwards to form cristae.
The inner space is called the matrix and contains enzymes involved in cellular respiration.
Mitochondria are the sites of aerobic cellular respiration and produce ATP, making energy available to the cell.
Diagram construction: draw an oval about 6 cm long and 3 cm wide for the outer membrane.
Draw a second oval about 5 cm long and 2 cm wide inside it for the inner membrane; show several inward folds of this membrane as cristae.
Label the outer membrane, inner membrane, cristae and matrix.

items.followUp: Give two examples of enzymes used in industry and state their uses.

rubric.why: Recognises enzyme use in cleaning products.
rubric.description: Enzymes such as proteases and lipases are added to detergents to help remove protein or fat stains.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct detergent use and its purpose.

rubric.why: Recognises enzyme use in food processing.
rubric.description: Enzymes are used in food processing, for example rennin in cheese-making.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct food-industry use.

rubric.why: Recognises other industrial applications of enzymes.
rubric.description: Enzymes are used in industries such as leather, textile or paper processing to treat materials.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming a correct industrial application and describing its use.

rubric.why: Credits a further valid use of enzymes.
rubric.description: Enzymes are also used in medicine, research or other industries, for example in diagnosis or in carrying out specific chemical processes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for another correct use with a relevant purpose.

modelAnswer: In detergents, enzymes such as proteases and lipases help break down protein and fat stains.
In food processing, enzymes such as rennin are used to make cheese.
In the leather and textile industries, enzymes help process and treat materials.
In medicine, enzymes are used in diagnostic tests and other medical applications.

items.followUp: Explain how carbon dioxide and water are used to make glucose during photosynthesis.

rubric.why: States how chlorophyll captures light energy.
rubric.description: Chlorophyll absorbs or traps light energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that chlorophyll captures light.

rubric.why: Explains the role of captured light energy in photosynthesis.
rubric.description: The absorbed light energy is converted into chemical energy used in photosynthesis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking absorbed light energy to the chemical process/energy of photosynthesis.

rubric.why: Includes the light-driven splitting of water.
rubric.description: Light energy enables water to split into hydrogen and oxygen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that water is split and identifying the products or naming photolysis.

rubric.why: Explains how the raw materials contribute to making food.
rubric.description: Hydrogen from water is used with carbon dioxide to form glucose or carbohydrate.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking carbon dioxide and hydrogen to the formation of glucose/carbohydrate.

rubric.why: Identifies the fate of oxygen formed from water.
rubric.description: Oxygen produced during water splitting is released as a by-product.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that oxygen is released.

modelAnswer: Chlorophyll in the leaves absorbs or traps light energy from the Sun.
The absorbed light energy is converted into chemical energy used in photosynthesis.
This energy enables water to split into hydrogen and oxygen.
Hydrogen from water combines with carbon dioxide to form glucose, which the plant uses or stores as food.
Oxygen formed from water is released as a by-product.
